IAM in ActionEnterprise Security How IAM Works Companies deploy IAM systems to control employee access to critical data. These systems verify identities and enforce permissions based on job roles. Real-World Example When employees log into the company intranet, SSO systems authenticate their credentials. The IAM framework then grants access to specific resources based on predetermined role permissions. An illustration of a modern office environment. Two people, a man and a woman, are seated at a long desk, viewed from behind. They are working on laptops. In front of them is a large wall-mounted screen displaying a 'Welcome!' message. Above the screen, a text box explains that the SSO system authenticates users and grants access based on role permissions. The screen itself shows a login form with fields for 'Full Name', 'Email Address', and 'City/State', and a 'Welcome logo' button. The overall color scheme is purple and pink. Illustration of two employees working at a desk with a large screen displaying a 'Welcome!' message and login options.

IGA vs AM The diagram illustrates the relationship between Identity Management (IGA) and Access Management (AM) across three phases: Before, During (runtime), and After. Identity Management (IGA) is associated with the Before phase. It involves managing identity, designing policies, approving access, and modeling roles. Authentication and Authorization are associated with the During (runtime) phase. This phase involves enforcing access decisions. Accounting is associated with the After phase. It involves reviewing logs, certifying access, and generating audit reports. The diagram shows that IGA is primarily concerned with the Before phase, while AM is primarily concerned with the During (runtime) phase. Accounting is a cross-cutting concern that spans across all three phases. Mini-Quiz 2 Which of the following is an example of Authentication? A) Checking user permissions for a resource B) Entering a password to verify identity C) Reviewing user activity logs D) Assigning a user to an admin group Answer: B) Entering a password to verify identity

Practice Overview Goal: Understand separation of responsibilities The diagram illustrates the separation of responsibilities in an IAM system. It features three main components: MidPoint (IGA), Keycloak (AM), and an LDAP Directory, with an additional LDAP Admin UI. MidPoint (IGA) : Contains an Identity Store and Business Roles. It is associated with a PostgreSQL database. Keycloak (AM) : Contains Authentication, LDAP Federation, OIDC Tokens, and Session Management. It is also associated with a PostgreSQL database. LDAP Directory : A central directory containing User Accounts and Groups (admins, managers, users). LDAP Admin : A UI for LDAP management. Interactions are shown as follows: A large blue arrow labeled "LDAP Resource Provisioning" points from MidPoint (IGA) to the LDAP Directory. A blue arrow labeled "LDAP Federation" points from the LDAP Directory to Keycloak (AM). A small blue arrow points from the LDAP Directory to the LDAP Admin UI. Diagram illustrating the separation of responsibilities in an IAM system.

midPoint Open Source IGA The diagram illustrates the architecture of midPoint, an Open Source Identity Governance (IGA) solution. At the top, an administrator (represented by a stick figure) interacts with the GUI (Graphical User Interface). The GUI is part of the midPoint core, which is represented by a large green block. Inside this core, the IDM logic (Identity Management logic) is shown as a central component. The midPoint core is connected to four external systems via connectors: HR connector : Connects midPoint to the HR (Human Resources) system. AD connector : Connects midPoint to the Active Directory (AD). DB connector : Connects midPoint to a Database (DB) and an Application . DMS connector : Connects midPoint to a DMS application (Document Management System). The connectors are shown as white boxes with labels, and the external systems are represented by various icons (blue rectangles for HR and DMS application, a blue cylinder for Active Directory, and a blue cylinder and rectangle for the Database and Application). Architecture diagram of midPoint showing its components and connections.

To the left, a User (represented by a cartoon person at a computer) interacts with Applications (represented by a server icon) via SSO (Single Sign-On). A large double-headed arrow labeled Authentication connects the User and Applications to the Keycloak component. To the right, Identity Brokering is shown, connecting Keycloak to Social login options: Sign in with Google , Sign in with GitHub , and Sign in with Facebook . Keycloak Architecture Diagram
